solution.concept_anchor: Nyaya school — four Pramanas
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c names six Pramanas, which correctly describes Mimamsa and Vedanta, not Nyaya, making it plausible for students who conflate these schools.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: Charvaka accepts only Pratyaksha (one Pramana), not a description of Nyaya.
Eliminate option c: Six Pramanas belong to Mimamsa/Vedanta, not Nyaya.
Eliminate option d: Samkhya accepts three Pramanas; this misidentifies Nyaya.
Confirm option b: Nyaya accepts exactly four Pramanas — Pratyaksha, Anumana, Upamana, and Shabda.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Many students recall that Nyaya is a logic-heavy school and assume it accepts fewer Pramanas, often confusing it with Samkhya (three) or inflating it to six like Mimamsa. The trap here is the scope of valid sources — Nyaya uniquely adds Upamana (analogy) as a distinct fourth Pramana, something other schools fold into inference or reject altogether. A student who has only partially studied this topic will likely mark either two or three.
solution.final_explanation:
Nyaya is primarily an epistemological school, and its framework of valid knowledge sources (Pramanas) is central to its philosophy. Nyaya accepts exactly four Pramanas.

• Option (a): Charvaka accepts only Pratyaksha — this is the materialist school's strict empiricism, not Nyaya.
• Option (b): Correct. Nyaya's four Pramanas are Pratyaksha (perception), Anumana (inference), Upamana (comparison/analogy), and Shabda (authoritative testimony). Upamana is Nyaya's distinctive contribution.
• Option (c): Six Pramanas — adding Arthapatti (postulation) and Anupalabdhi (non-apprehension) — characterise Mimamsa and Advaita Vedanta.
• Option (d): Three Pramanas (Pratyaksha, Anumana, Shabda) describe the Samkhya school.

Value Addition:
• Shabda in Nyaya specifically means reliable testimony, including Vedic authority.
• Upamana involves knowing a new object by its similarity to a known object — e.g., learning what a wild cow (gavaya) looks like by being told it resembles a domestic cow.
• Charvaka's rejection of Anumana (inference) is the basis of its philosophical materialism.

solution.concept_anchor: Vaisheshika Padarthas — six original, seventh later

statement_analysis.statement: The original six Padarthas enumerated by Kanada include Dravya, Guna, Karma, Samanya, Vishesha, and Samavaya.
statement_analysis.reason: Kanada's Vaisheshika Sutras enumerate precisely these six categories as the fundamental ontological divisions of reality.

statement_analysis.statement: Abhava (non-existence) was included as the seventh Padartha by Kanada himself in the Vaisheshika Sutras.
statement_analysis.reason: Abhava was added as a seventh category by later commentators, not by Kanada in his original Sutras.

statement_analysis.statement: The name 'Vaisheshika' is derived from the category 'Vishesha', which refers to the ultimate differentiators of eternal substances.
statement_analysis.reason: Vishesha (ultimate particulars) is the distinctive ontological contribution of this school, and the school takes its name from this category.

solution.strong_distractor: d — A student who knows Abhava exists as a category but is unaware it was a later addition will mark all three as correct, making option d the strongest trap.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: The six original Padarthas are textbook Vaisheshika — Statement 1 is correct.
Examine Statement 2 carefully: The phrase 'by Kanada himself' is the trap — Abhava was added by later commentators, making Statement 2 incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: 'Vaisheshika' derives from 'Vishesha' — this is the etymological origin of the school's name, so Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option c (1 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is designed to catch students who know Abhava is part of Vaisheshika ontology but do not recall that it was a post-Kanada addition. The qualifier 'by Kanada himself' is the critical phrase. Many students study the seven categories as a unified system and do not distinguish between the original six and the later addition, causing them to mark Statement 2 as correct and choose option d.
solution.final_explanation:
The Vaisheshika school organises all of reality into fundamental categories called Padarthas. Kanada's original system had six.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The six Padarthas in Kanada's Vaisheshika Sutras are Dravya (substance), Guna (quality), Karma (action), Samanya (universal), Vishesha (particular), and Samavaya (inherence). These cover all positive existents.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Abhava (non-existence) was introduced as a seventh Padartha by later Vaisheshika commentators, not by Kanada in the original Sutras.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The school's name literally means 'that which deals with Vishesha' — the ultimate differentiators that distinguish eternal atoms from one another.

Value Addition:
• Samavaya (inherence) is particularly important — it is the inseparable relationship between substance and its qualities.
• The seven Padarthas together cover both positive being (Bhava) and non-being (Abhava).
• Vishesha applies only to eternal substances (nitya dravyas) like atoms and Atman — not to composite objects.

solution.concept_anchor: Vaisheshika atomic substances — which four elements

statement_analysis.statement: Earth (Prithvi) is constituted by atoms (Paramanu) according to Vaisheshika.
statement_analysis.reason: Earth is one of the four elements whose ultimate units are atoms in Vaisheshika — atoms of earth combine to form gross earth.

statement_analysis.statement: Ether (Akasha) is constituted by atoms according to Vaisheshika.
statement_analysis.reason: Akasha is explicitly non-atomic in Vaisheshika — it is eternal and all-pervading, not made of atoms; only Earth, Water, Fire, and Air are atomic.

statement_analysis.statement: Mind (Manas) is constituted by atoms according to Vaisheshika.
statement_analysis.reason: Manas is described as atomic in size (anu) but is not made of Paramanu in the same sense — it is a single, eternal, non-composite substance; it is not formed by atomic combination like the four elements.

statement_analysis.statement: Water (Jala) is constituted by atoms (Paramanu) according to Vaisheshika.
statement_analysis.reason: Water is one of the four atomic elements — its atoms combine through Dvyanuka (dyads) and Tryanuka (triads) to form perceptible water.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who recall that Manas is described as 'anu' (atomic-sized) in Vaisheshika may incorrectly count it among the atomic elements, raising the count to three.
elimination_logic: Identify atomic elements in Vaisheshika: only Earth, Water, Fire, and Air — the four bhautic elements.
Eliminate Akasha: it is eternal, all-pervading, and explicitly non-atomic — a single substance not formed by combination.
Eliminate Manas on careful reading: though described as atom-sized, Manas is not formed by atomic combination — it is an eternal individual substance.
Earth and Water are correctly identified as atomic — only two of the four statements are correct, select option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Manas in Vaisheshika is described as 'anu' (infinitesimally small), which many students conflate with being composed of Paramanu like the four elements. This is a critical distinction: Manas is atomic in size but is a singular, eternal, non-composite substance. The trap exploits identical vocabulary used in different senses.
solution.final_explanation:
Vaisheshika's atomic theory applies only to four of the nine substances. Consider the following pairs regarding atomic constitution:

| Substance | Atomic (Paramanu)? |
|---|---|
| Earth (Prithvi) | Yes |
| Ether (Akasha) | No |
| Mind (Manas) | No |
| Water (Jala) | Yes |

• Earth — Correct: One of the four atomic elements.
• Akasha — Incorrect: All-pervading, eternal, and non-atomic; a single continuous substance.
• Manas — Incorrect: Though infinitesimally small ('anu'), it is not formed by Paramanu combination — each individual has one indivisible Manas.
• Water — Correct: Atomic; Dvyanuka (two atoms) and Tryanuka (three atoms) lead to perceptible water.

Only two pairs are correctly matched — option b.

Value Addition:
• The five non-atomic substances are Akasha, Kala (Time), Dik (Space), Atman (Self), and Manas.
• Atomic combination is the Vaisheshika explanation for change and causation.
• This is distinct from modern atomic theory — no empirical verification is claimed.

solution.concept_anchor: Vaisheshika relational categories — Samavaya vs Samyoga
solution.strong_distractor: b — Confusing Samavaya with Samyoga (both are relational concepts) causes students to swap A and B, landing on option b.
elimination_logic: Identify Samavaya (A): It is inseparable inherence — e.g., a quality in a substance cannot be physically separated; this maps to item 3.
Identify Samyoga (B): It is mere contact or conjunction — separable; e.g., a book on a table; this maps to item 1.
Identify Karma (C): Action or motion — the dynamic category causing change; maps to item 4.
Identify Guna (D): Quality or attribute — e.g., colour, taste; maps to item 2. This gives A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — option d.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Samavaya and Samyoga are both relational concepts in Vaisheshika and are frequently confused. The trap conflates them: Samyoga is external, separable contact, while Samavaya is intrinsic, inseparable inherence. A student who knows both exist but has not memorised their precise definitions will likely swap them, landing on option b or c.
solution.final_explanation:
Vaisheshika distinguishes between different kinds of relationships among its categories. Matching correctly requires understanding the precise definition of each:

• A (Samavaya) — 3 (Inseparable inherence between substance and quality): Samavaya is the permanent, inseparable bond — e.g., colour cannot exist apart from the substance it colours.
• B (Samyoga) — 1 (Separable conjunctive contact between two substances): Samyoga is external contact — a hand touching a fruit; they can be separated.
• C (Karma) — 4 (Action or motion that brings about change): Karma in Vaisheshika denotes physical motion — upward, downward, expansion, contraction, locomotion.
• D (Guna) — 2 (Attribute that inheres in a substance): Guna includes properties like colour, taste, smell, number, and size.

The trap pairing is A/B — students must distinguish inherence (inseparable) from contact (separable).

Value Addition:
• Samavaya is itself one of the six original Padarthas, while Samyoga is a type of Guna (quality).
• There are 24 Gunas listed in Vaisheshika — a frequently examined detail.
• Karma in Vaisheshika is physical motion, entirely distinct from the Vedantic/karmic sense.

solution.concept_anchor: Nyaya-Vaisheshika textual lineage sequence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Tattvachintamani is a medieval text but confuse Prasastapada's commentary as being later than Vatsyayana's may select option c.
elimination_logic: Anchor Gangesa's Tattvachintamani to the 13th century CE — this is the latest text and must come last.
Kanada's Vaisheshika Sutras are foundational and ancient — they must come first among these four.

Vatsyayana's Nyaya Bhashya is a commentary on Gautama's Nyaya Sutras and is dated to approximately 4th–5th century CE; Prasastapada's Padarthadharmasangraha is also 4th–6th century CE but slightly later than Vatsyayana.
Correct order: Kanada → Vatsyayana → Prasastapada → Gangesa — option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the relative placement of Vatsyayana and Prasastapada. Both are commentators of the post-Sutra ancient period, and students often guess their order. Kanada's primacy and Gangesa's medieval date are well known, but the middle placement is where errors occur.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the textual lineage of Nyaya and Vaisheshika requires knowing the approximate historical placement of key texts.

Correct order: Kanada (Vaisheshika Sutras) → Vatsyayana (Nyaya Bhashya, c. 4th–5th CE) → Prasastapada (Padarthadharmasangraha, c. 6th CE) → Gangesa (Tattvachintamani, c. 13th CE).

• Kanada's Vaisheshika Sutras are the foundational text of the school — ancient, pre-CE or early CE.
• Vatsyayana's Nyaya Bhashya is the primary commentary on Gautama's Nyaya Sutras — 4th–5th century CE.
• Prasastapada's Padarthadharmasangraha systematises the Vaisheshika categories — 6th century CE.
• Gangesa's Tattvachintamani inaugurates the Navya-Nyaya (New Logic) school — 13th century CE.

Value Addition:
• Gautama (Akshapada) authored the Nyaya Sutras before all these commentators.
• Navya-Nyaya developed a technical metalanguage that influenced Indian scholarship across disciplines.
• Gangesa's school flourished in Mithila and later in Nabadwip (Bengal).

solution.concept_anchor: Asatkaryavada vs Satkaryavada schools
solution.strong_distractor: b — Nyaya is often grouped with Vaisheshika as a sister school, so students may assume it also holds a different theory of causation from Samkhya, forgetting that Nyaya-Vaisheshika shares Asatkaryavada.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: which schools hold Asatkaryavada (effect is new, not pre-existent in cause)?
Vaisheshika holds Asatkaryavada — effect (e.g., a pot) is genuinely new, not pre-existent in clay.
Nyaya shares this Asatkaryavada position with Vaisheshika — they form an allied school.
Mimamsa also holds a version of Asatkaryavada (Arambhavada).
Samkhya holds Satkaryavada — the effect pre-exists in the cause — making it the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students may not recall that Nyaya also holds Asatkaryavada, assuming Nyaya and Vaisheshika differ on this issue. This causes them to overlook Samkhya as the odd one out and incorrectly eliminate Nyaya instead.
solution.final_explanation:
The debate over whether an effect pre-exists in its cause (Satkaryavada) or is genuinely new (Asatkaryavada) is one of the most important in Indian metaphysics.

• Option (a) Vaisheshika: Holds Asatkaryavada — a pot is genuinely new after a potter shapes clay; the effect did not pre-exist. Belongs to the group.
• Option (b) Nyaya: Also holds Asatkaryavada (called Arambhavada) — allied with Vaisheshika. Belongs to the group.
• Option (c) Samkhya: Holds Satkaryavada — the effect pre-exists in the cause in an unmanifest form; creation is merely manifestation. This is the ODD ONE OUT.
• Option (d) Mimamsa: Also holds Arambhavada/Asatkaryavada. Belongs to the group.

Value Addition:
• Advaita Vedanta holds Vivartavada — the world is an appearance (not a real transformation) of Brahman.
• Vishishtadvaita holds Parinamavada — Brahman genuinely transforms into the world.
• Samkhya's Satkaryavada supports its cosmology: Prakriti evolves (Parinama) into the 23 tattvas.

solution.concept_anchor: Nyaya-Vaisheshika pluralist Atman vs Advaita

statement_analysis.statement: Nyaya-Vaisheshika accepts multiple individual Atmans, each eternally distinct — a pluralistic position that contrasts with Advaita Vedanta's single Brahman.
statement_analysis.reason: Vaisheshika lists Atman as one of the nine Dravyas and explicitly accepts multiple individual souls, making it a pluralistic realist school — directly opposed to Advaita's non-dualism.

statement_analysis.statement: In the Nyaya-Vaisheshika system, Atman is inherently conscious — consciousness is its essential nature, not an accidental property.
statement_analysis.reason: In Nyaya-Vaisheshika, consciousness (Jnana) is an accidental/contingent property of Atman — it arises when Atman is connected to the body and Manas; the liberated Atman in Apavarga has no consciousness, showing consciousness is not Atman's essential nature.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students familiar with Vedantic ideas may assume all Astika schools share the same view of Atman as pure consciousness, making Statement 2 appear correct.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Multiple individual Atmans as pluralistic realism is a core Nyaya-Vaisheshika teaching — Statement 1 is correct.

Examine Statement 2: In Nyaya-Vaisheshika, the liberated Atman (in Apavarga state) has no consciousness — this shows consciousness is not Atman's essential nature but an accidental property arising from bodily connection.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect — select option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the assumption that all Astika schools share the Vedantic view of Atman as pure consciousness. In Nyaya-Vaisheshika, this is false — consciousness arises contingently and is absent in the liberated state, showing it is not Atman's essential nature.
solution.final_explanation:
The Nyaya-Vaisheshika concept of Atman differs significantly from Vedantic notions.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Nyaya-Vaisheshika is explicitly pluralistic — multiple individual Atmans exist eternally. Each person, and indeed each living being, has a distinct Atman. This contrasts sharply with Advaita Vedanta's Eka Brahman (one reality) and with Buddhism's Anatman (no-self).
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Consciousness is not the essential nature of Atman in this school. In the liberated state (Apavarga), the Atman is freed from all pain but also from all conscious experience — it is described as 'stone-like.' This makes consciousness an adventitious property, not the intrinsic mark of Atman.

Value Addition:
• This 'unconscious liberation' is one of the most criticised aspects of Nyaya-Vaisheshika from a Vedantic perspective.
• Atman in Vaisheshika is the substratum of desire (Iccha), effort (Prayatna), pleasure, pain, and cognition — all contingent properties.
• Buddhism denies Atman altogether (Anatman) — Nyaya actively refuted this position.

concepts_used: Navya-Nyaya (New Logic) School

solution.concept_anchor: Gangesa — Tattvachintamani — Navya-Nyaya
solution.strong_distractor: c — Vatsyayana is a well-known Nyaya scholar, and students may confuse him as the founder of Navya-Nyaya, not realising he predates this medieval reform by nearly a millennium.
elimination_logic: Identify the text: Tattvachintamani is the defining work of the Navya-Nyaya (New Logic) school — this is a specific fact.
Eliminate option a: Udayana authored Nyayakusumanjali — a theistic proof text, not the Navya-Nyaya foundational text.
Eliminate option c: Vatsyayana authored Nyaya Bhashya — a commentary on Gautama's Sutras, not Tattvachintamani.
Eliminate option d: Prasastapada authored Padarthadharmasangraha in the Vaisheshika tradition — not Tattvachintamani.
Confirm option b: Gangesa Upadhyaya of the 13th century CE authored Tattvachintamani, founding Navya-Nyaya.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Udayana is a strong distractor because he is the most prominent Nyaya logician before Gangesa and is associated with Nyayakusumanjali. Students conflate his prominence with authorship of Tattvachintamani, which in fact belongs to Gangesa.
solution.final_explanation:
The Navya-Nyaya (New Logic) school represents a medieval reformation of the original Nyaya school, developed with a highly technical logical vocabulary.

• Option (a) Udayana: Authored the Nyayakusumanjali — famous for logical proofs of God's existence. Not the author of Tattvachintamani.
• Option (b) Gangesa Upadhyaya: Correct. The 13th century CE scholar from Mithila who authored Tattvachintamani, founding Navya-Nyaya with a precise metalanguage for epistemological analysis.
• Option (c) Vatsyayana: Authored the Nyaya Bhashya — the primary commentary on Gautama's Nyaya Sutras. An earlier scholar, not associated with Navya-Nyaya.
• Option (d) Prasastapada: Authored the Padarthadharmasangraha — the primary Vaisheshika commentary, not a Nyaya text.

Value Addition:
• Navya-Nyaya's technical language influenced Sanskrit grammar, Mimamsa, and later Vedanta.
• The school flourished in Nabadwip (Bengal) after Mithila.
• Tattvachintamani deals with the four Pramanas with unprecedented logical rigour.

Vaisheshika's Atomic Theory (Paramanu Vada)

solution.concept_anchor: Kanada — philosophical atomic theory distinction
solution.strong_distractor: b — Stating that Kanada's atomic theory anticipated modern chemistry appeals to nationalist historiography and is a widely circulated claim that is technically false in a philosophically precise sense.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: Kanada authored the Vaisheshika Sutras, not the Nyaya Sutras — those belong to Gautama (Akshapada).
Eliminate option b: Kanada's atomic theory is philosophical/metaphysical — it was not derived from empirical experimentation and cannot be equated with modern atomic science.
Eliminate option c: Kanada is also called Uluka — the name 'Kanada' relates to grain-eating (kana = grain particle), not to the concept of atoms.
Confirm option d: Kanada's atoms are eternal, indivisible, and imperceptible — these are correct attributes of Paramanu in Vaisheshika.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option b exploits the popular claim that Kanada 'discovered atomic theory' — while he theorised indivisible particles, the theory is metaphysical and non-empirical. Option c exploits the plausible-sounding etymology connecting 'Kanada' to atoms, when the actual derivation relates to grain-eating.
solution.final_explanation:
Kanada (also called Uluka) is the founder of the Vaisheshika school.

• Option (a): Incorrectly pairs Kanada with the Nyaya Sutras. The Nyaya Sutras were authored by Gautama (Akshapada). Kanada authored the Vaisheshika Sutras.
• Option (b): Incorrectly describes Kanada's atomic theory as empirical science anticipating modern chemistry. It is a metaphysical/philosophical theory arrived at through reasoning, not experimentation.
• Option (c): Incorrectly states 'Kanada' derives from the word for atom. 'Kanada' means grain-eater (kana = grain/small particle), referring to his ascetic practice of surviving on grain particles — the name has a biographical, not philosophical, origin.
• Option (d): Correct. Paramanu in Vaisheshika are eternal (nitya), indivisible (further analysis impossible), and imperceptible to ordinary senses — only inferred through their effects.

Value Addition:
• Kanada's other name Uluka means 'owl' — both names carry legendary significance.
• Atoms of different elements (earth, water, fire, air) are qualitatively distinct in Vaisheshika.
• Two atoms combine to form a Dvyanuka (dyad), the smallest perceptible unit.

solution.concept_anchor: Tarka — not an independent Pramana in Nyaya

statement_analysis.statement: Tarka (hypothetical reasoning/reductio ad absurdum) is recognised as an independent Pramana in the Nyaya system alongside Pratyaksha and Anumana.
statement_analysis.reason: Tarka supports inference but is not an independent Pramana in Nyaya — the school recognises exactly four Pramanas (Pratyaksha, Anumana, Upamana, Shabda), and Tarka is not among them.

statement_analysis.statement: Nyaya's theory of debate distinguishes between Vada (honest dialectic seeking truth) and Vitanda (a form of debate aimed solely at refuting the opponent without establishing an alternative thesis).
statement_analysis.reason: Nyaya's Vadavidya (theory of debate) explicitly classifies three types: Vada (honest), Jalpa (disputative with victory as goal), and Vitanda (purely destructive/sophistic).

statement_analysis.statement: Jalpa, one of the three debate forms in Nyaya, permits the use of fallacies (Hetvabhasa) and sophistry to win an argument, distinguishing it from Vada.
statement_analysis.reason: Jalpa is the competitive form of debate where the goal is winning, not truth — it permits sophistic moves; this contrasts with Vada, which follows strict logical rules.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know Tarka is important in Nyaya logic often assume it must be a Pramana, making option d (all three correct) appear plausible.
elimination_logic: Examine Statement 1: The claim that Tarka is an 'independent Pramana' is false — Nyaya has exactly four Pramanas, and Tarka is not one of them; it only assists inference.
Verify Statement 2: Nyaya's three debate types include Vada and Vitanda as described — Statement 2 is correct.
Verify Statement 3: Jalpa is characterised by its allowance of sophistry in service of winning — this is accurate Nyaya debate theory.
Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct — select option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits Tarka's prominence in Nyaya logical discourse. Students who see Tarka discussed extensively in epistemological texts assume it must be a Pramana. The trap is the qualifier 'independent' — Tarka is a supporting analytical tool, not a standalone source of valid knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
Nyaya's contributions to debate theory (Vadavidya) are as significant as its epistemology.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Tarka is an indirect reasoning tool (hypothetical/reductio ad absurdum) that strengthens inference, but Nyaya does not count it as a fifth Pramana. The four Pramanas remain fixed at Pratyaksha, Anumana, Upamana, and Shabda.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Vada is honest dialectical debate aimed at establishing truth through valid argument. Vitanda is purely destructive — the debater refutes without offering an alternative view.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Jalpa is the 'competitive' debate form — victory-oriented, permitting fallacies (Hetvabhasa) and deceptive moves not allowed in Vada.

Value Addition:
• The 16 categories (Padarthas) of Nyaya include topics like Pramana, Prameya, Hetvabhasa, Tarka, Nirnaya — a broader list than Vaisheshika's Padarthas.
• Hetvabhasa (fallacies of inference) is a major Nyaya contribution — five types are listed.
• Vitanda is associated with Sophists in Greek philosophy — a cross-civilisational parallel.

solution.concept_anchor: Vaisheshika nine Dravyas — which are eternal

statement_analysis.statement: Akasha (Ether) is eternal (nitya) in Vaisheshika.
statement_analysis.reason: Akasha is one of the five non-atomic, all-pervading eternal substances in Vaisheshika — it is singular, continuous, and not subject to destruction.

statement_analysis.statement: A pot made of clay is eternal (nitya) in Vaisheshika.
statement_analysis.reason: Composite objects (Avayavi) like a pot are non-eternal (anitya) — they are formed by atomic combination and can be destroyed; only atoms themselves among material substances are eternal.

statement_analysis.statement: Individual Atman is eternal (nitya) in Vaisheshika.
statement_analysis.reason: Atman is one of the nine Dravyas and is explicitly eternal — it persists through multiple rebirths and is not destroyed even in liberation.

statement_analysis.statement: Manas (Mind) is eternal (nitya) in Vaisheshika.
statement_analysis.reason: Each individual Manas is an eternal, atomic-sized substance that mediates between Atman and the sense organs; it is not created or destroyed.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know composite objects are non-eternal but are uncertain about Manas's status may count only two eternal substances (Akasha and Atman), landing on option b.
elimination_logic: Identify eternal substances in Vaisheshika: atoms of four elements, Akasha, Kala, Dik, Atman, and Manas are all eternal in their fundamental form.
Statement 1 — Akasha: eternal (non-atomic, all-pervading) — correct.
Statement 2 — A clay pot: a composite (Avayavi) object — non-eternal — incorrect.
Statements 3 and 4 — Atman and Manas: both are explicitly eternal in Vaisheshika — correct.
Three of four statements are correct — select option c (Only three).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 traps students who confuse earth atoms (eternal) with a clay pot (non-eternal composite). The Vaisheshika system is precise: it is the Paramanu that is eternal, not the composite objects formed from them. A student reading 'clay' and thinking 'earth element' will incorrectly mark Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Vaisheshika distinguishes eternal (nitya) substances from non-eternal (anitya) ones. Among the nine Dravyas:

| Substance | Eternal? |
|---|---|
| Akasha (Ether) | Yes |
| A clay pot | No |
| Individual Atman | Yes |
| Manas (Mind) | Yes |

• Akasha — Correct: Eternal, singular, all-pervading — not made of atoms.
• A clay pot — Incorrect: It is a composite (Avayavi) — non-eternal; earth atoms are eternal but their combinations are not.
• Atman — Correct: Eternal individual soul; persists through rebirths.
• Manas — Correct: Eternal, indivisible, atomic-sized mind-stuff in each individual.

Three of four are correctly described as eternal — option c.

Value Addition:
• The distinction between eternal atoms and non-eternal composites is the foundation of Vaisheshika causation theory.
• Kala (Time) and Dik (Space) are also eternal — both singular and all-pervading.
• This pluralistic list of nine eternal types contrasts sharply with Advaita's single Brahman.

solution.concept_anchor: Nyaya Alaukika perception — three types

statement_analysis.statement: Nyaya school recognises only Laukika (ordinary) perception and does not accept any form of extraordinary perception (Alaukika Pratyaksha).
statement_analysis.reason: Nyaya explicitly accepts Alaukika (extraordinary) perception in three forms: Samanyalakshana, Jnanalakshana, and Yogaja — making this statement false.

statement_analysis.statement: Nirvikalpa (indeterminate) perception in Nyaya refers to the bare, unqualified apprehension of an object without any relational judgment or name.
statement_analysis.reason: Nirvikalpa perception is the immediate, pre-judgmental contact with an object — it grasps the bare 'this' without attributing qualities or relations; this is accurately described.

statement_analysis.statement: Yogaja perception in Nyaya refers to the extraordinary cognitive power attained by yogis through meditative practice, enabling them to directly perceive imperceptible objects.
statement_analysis.reason: Yogaja is one of the three Alaukika perceptions — it is the direct cognitive access gained by accomplished yogis, enabling perception of atoms, past events, and others' minds.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Nyaya is an empiricist-adjacent school may assume it rejects extraordinary perception as unscientific, making Statement 1 appear correct and Statement 2 the error.
elimination_logic: Assess Statement 1: The claim that Nyaya recognises ONLY ordinary perception is false — Nyaya explicitly lists three types of extraordinary (Alaukika) perception; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Assess Statement 2: Nirvikalpa perception as pre-judgmental bare apprehension is standard Nyaya epistemology — Statement 2 is correct.
Assess Statement 3: Yogaja perception as yogi's direct cognition is one of the three Alaukika types — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statement 1 is incorrect — select option b (1 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the intuition that Nyaya, being logic-focused, would restrict perception to ordinary sensory experience. This is incorrect — Nyaya is not a strict empiricist school and accepts extraordinary perception. Students who project modern empiricism onto Nyaya will incorrectly validate Statement 1.
solution.final_explanation:
Nyaya's theory of perception is richer than many students expect. It accepts two major types of Pratyaksha.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Nyaya accepts three types of Alaukika (extraordinary) perception: Samanyalakshana (perception of a universal through a particular), Jnanalakshana (perception of one object's qualities through another sense), and Yogaja (yogi's direct perception). The claim that Nyaya accepts only ordinary perception is false.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Nirvikalpa perception is the pre-relational, pre-linguistic bare awareness — pure contact before any judgment like 'this is a red flower.' It grasps existence without predication.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Yogaja is the extraordinary perceptual capacity of advanced yogis — they can perceive atoms, the past, the future, and even others' mental states directly.

Value Addition:
• Samanyalakshana: perceiving 'cowness' directly through seeing one cow — a controversial Nyaya claim.
• Jnanalakshana: perceiving the coldness of ice by seeing it — crossing sensory channels.
• Savikalpa (determinate) perception involves relational judgments and is what ordinary language describes.

solution.concept_anchor: Four types of Abhava in Vaisheshika
solution.strong_distractor: b — Pragabhava and Pradhvamsabhava are both temporal forms of Abhava and students frequently swap them, not distinguishing prior non-existence from posterior non-existence.
elimination_logic: Identify Pragabhava (A): 'Praga' means 'before' — prior non-existence of the effect before it is produced (e.g., non-existence of a pot before it is made); maps to item 2.
Identify Pradhvamsabhava (B): 'Pradhvamsa' means 'destruction' — posterior non-existence after an object is destroyed (e.g., non-existence of a broken pot after breaking); maps to item 4.
Identify Anyonyabhava (C): 'Anyonya' means 'mutual' — mutual non-existence, the difference between two existing things (a cow is not a horse and vice versa); maps to item 1.

Identify Atyantabhava (D): 'Atyanta' means 'absolute/eternal' — absolute non-existence of something that never exists anywhere (e.g., sky-flower); maps to item 3. This gives A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 — option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Pragabhava and Pradhvamsabhava are the critical trap — both are temporal. Students who know them as 'prior' and 'posterior' non-existence but haven't fixed which is which will swap them. Option b (swapping these two) is specifically designed to catch this error.
solution.final_explanation:
Vaisheshika treats Abhava (non-existence) as a genuine ontological category with four sub-types:

• A (Pragabhava) — 2 (Non-existence of an effect before it is produced): Prior non-existence. A pot does not exist before the potter makes it. This non-existence has no beginning but has an end.
• B (Pradhvamsabhava) — 4 (Non-existence of something after it is destroyed): Posterior non-existence. After a pot is broken, the pot's non-existence begins. This has a beginning but no end.
• C (Anyonyabhava) — 1 (Mutual non-existence between two co-existing entities): A cow is not a horse and a horse is not a cow — each is mutually absent from the other.
• D (Atyantabhava) — 3 (Absolute non-existence of something that never exists at any time): Sky-flower (Kha-pushpa) — never exists anywhere, anytime. Neither beginning nor end.

Value Addition:
• Pragabhava is beginningless but ends; Pradhvamsabhava begins but is endless.
• Atyantabhava is the strongest — used in logical refutation of impossible entities.
• This categorisation shows Vaisheshika's ambition to make ontology exhaustive — covering even non-being.

concepts_used: Nyaya-Vaisheshika Synthesis and Their Complementary Relationship
Classification of Nyaya and Vaisheshika within Astika Schools

solution.concept_anchor: Nyaya epistemology + Vaisheshika ontology — complementary merger
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the historical merger occurred and that Nyaya epistemology supports Vaisheshika metaphysics may assume the causal relationship in R correctly explains A without critically examining the direction.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Nyaya's primary focus is epistemology/logic (how we know), and Vaisheshika's is ontology/metaphysics (what exists). This is the standard academic characterisation.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. By the medieval period, the two schools were routinely studied and treated as a single combined system (Nyaya-Vaisheshika).

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The complementary nature of their domains — one dealing with knowing, the other with being — is precisely what enabled and motivated their historical merger. The epistemological tools of Nyaya validate and support the ontological claims of Vaisheshika, making their union both natural and historically documented.
A correct + R correct + R explains A — select option a.
solution.final_explanation:
The Nyaya-Vaisheshika synthesis is one of the most significant developments in classical Indian philosophy.

Assertion (A): Nyaya is primarily an epistemological school — it asks how valid knowledge is obtained (Pramana theory, syllogism, perception). Vaisheshika is primarily ontological — it asks what categories of real existence there are (nine Dravyas, seven Padarthas, atomic theory). This division is accurate.

Reason (R): By the medieval period, these schools merged into a single system. Scholars like Udayana worked within both frameworks simultaneously. The complementarity is perfect: Nyaya provides the epistemological tools to know reality; Vaisheshika provides the ontological map of what reality consists of. R correctly explains why A is true — their merger was motivated precisely by their complementary domains.

Value Addition:
• The merged system is often called 'Nyaya-Vaisheshika' in medieval scholarship.
• Shared metaphysical commitments (pluralism, realism, theism) made the merger philosophically coherent.
• Both schools accepted the Vedas as authoritative testimony (Shabda Pramana), making them orthodox (Astika).
• Their opposition to Buddhist idealism and momentariness theory was another unifying factor.

solution.concept_anchor: Vaisheshika realism about universals — Samanya
solution.strong_distractor: c — Buddhist nominalism is a well-known alternative position and students who know Vaisheshika opposes Buddhism may not recall the specific realist vs nominalist dimension of that opposition.
elimination_logic: The question asks about Vaisheshika's position on universals — identify whether it is realist, nominalist, or conceptualist.
Eliminate option b: Conceptualism holds universals exist only in the mind — Vaisheshika rejects this and holds they exist independently in reality.
Eliminate option c: Nominalism denies real universals — this is the Buddhist position that Vaisheshika actively refuted.
Eliminate option d: Universals in Vaisheshika are not the same as individual atoms — Samanya is distinct from Vishesha.
Confirm option a: Vaisheshika holds that universals like 'cowness' exist objectively and independently in the external world — a realist position.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option c is designed to attract students who know Vaisheshika opposes Buddhism but do not recall the specific dimension of that opposition. The Buddhist nominalist position (universals are mere names) is exactly what Vaisheshika's Samanya theory refutes — making option c the most dangerous distractor.
solution.final_explanation:
The question of universals — whether properties like 'cowness' exist in reality or only in the mind — is a central debate in Indian philosophy.

• Option (a): Correct. Vaisheshika holds that universals (Samanya) are real, objective entities that exist independently in the world — a position called Realism. 'Cowness' is not just a mental label; it inheres in every cow as a real ontological entity.
• Option (b): Conceptualism — universals exist only as mental concepts — is not the Vaisheshika position.
• Option (c): Nominalism — universals are mere names (words) without real referents — is the Buddhist position that Vaisheshika actively refuted.
• Option (d): Confusing Samanya (universals) with Vishesha (ultimate particulars of atoms) reverses the Vaisheshika framework.

Value Addition:
• Samanya creates resemblances; Vishesha creates differences — together they explain why things are similar yet distinct.
• This realist position parallels Platonic realism in Western philosophy — a useful comparison.
• Vaisheshika's debate with Buddhists on universals was one of the defining polemics of classical Indian thought.

(b) Conceptualism — universals exist only as mental categories imposed by the mind on particulars
(c) Nominalism — universals are merely linguistic labels with no real counterpart in the world
(d) Atomism — universals are reducible to the aggregate properties of individual atoms

solution.concept_anchor: Gautama of Nyaya — not Gautama Buddha

statement_analysis.statement: The Nyaya Sutras were authored by Gautama (Akshapada), who is the same historical figure as Gautama Buddha — both texts reflect a common philosophical heritage.
statement_analysis.reason: Gautama (Akshapada), the author of Nyaya Sutras, is an entirely different person from Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha). Nyaya is an orthodox (Astika) school that accepts Vedic authority, while Buddhism explicitly rejects it — they represent opposing philosophical traditions.

statement_analysis.statement: Vatsyayana's Nyaya Bhashya is the primary commentary on the Nyaya Sutras of Gautama.
statement_analysis.reason: Vatsyayana's Nyaya Bhashya is indeed the foundational and most authoritative commentary on Gautama's Nyaya Sutras, dated to approximately the 4th–5th century CE.

statement_analysis.statement: The Padarthadharmasangraha of Prasastapada is a commentary on the Vaisheshika Sutras of Kanada.
statement_analysis.reason: Prasastapada's text is the defining systematic exposition of Vaisheshika categories and serves as the key commentary in the Vaisheshika tradition.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who correctly identify Statement 1 as false may second-guess themselves, thinking Statements 2 or 3 might also contain errors, leading to an over-correction.
elimination_logic: Scrutinise Statement 1: The claim that Gautama Akshapada and Gautama Buddha are the same person is factually false — Nyaya is Astika (Vedic) while Buddhism is Nastika.
Verify Statement 2: Vatsyayana as primary commentator on Nyaya Sutras is standard textbook knowledge — Statement 2 is correct.
Verify Statement 3: Prasastapada's Padarthadharmasangraha as key Vaisheshika commentary is established — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statement 1 is incorrect — select option b (1 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is the primary Gautama-confusion trap. The identical name used for both the Nyaya founder and the Buddha makes this a perennial source of error. Students with shallow preparation assume one Gautama across both traditions, not realising Nyaya and Buddhism are philosophically opposed on Vedic authority, God, and Atman.
solution.final_explanation:
The shared name 'Gautama' is one of the most tested traps in Indian philosophy questions.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Gautama Akshapada (Nyaya) and Siddhartha Gautama (Buddha) are entirely different historical figures. Nyaya is an Astika school that affirms Vedic authority; Buddhism (Nastika) explicitly denies it. They represent opposing metaphysical traditions — Nyaya accepted God and Atman; Buddhism rejected both.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Vatsyayana's Nyaya Bhashya is the principal commentary on Gautama's Nyaya Sutras — written around 4th–5th century CE, it remains the foundational interpretive text.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Prasastapada's Padarthadharmasangraha systematises the six Padarthas and is the key secondary text of Vaisheshika — though technically an independent treatise, it functions as the definitive commentary.

Value Addition:
• 'Akshapada' is another name for Gautama of Nyaya — meaning 'one whose eyes are at his feet.'
• Nyaya actively refuted Buddhist philosophical claims — especially through Udayana.
• The Nyaya Sutras are composed in five books (Adhyayas) covering 16 categories (Padarthas).

solution.concept_anchor: Asatkaryavada vs Satkaryavada — Vaisheshika vs Samkhya

statement_analysis.statement: According to Vaisheshika's theory of causation (Asatkaryavada), the effect is genuinely new and does not pre-exist in the cause.
statement_analysis.reason: Asatkaryavada (theory of non-pre-existence of the effect) is the defining causal theory of Vaisheshika — a pot is not hidden in clay; it is genuinely created. This contrasts with Samkhya.

statement_analysis.statement: Samkhya's Satkaryavada holds that an effect is a completely new creation unrelated to the causal substance, justifying the school's acceptance of creation ex nihilo.
statement_analysis.reason: Satkaryavada holds the exact opposite — the effect pre-exists in the cause in an unmanifest form; creation is only the manifestation (Vyakta) of what was already there (Avyakta). There is no creation ex nihilo in Samkhya.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both terms exist but are unsure which school holds which position may mark both statements as correct without verifying the substance of Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Asatkaryavada — effect is new — is correctly attributed to Vaisheshika; Statement 1 is correct.
Critically read Statement 2: Satkaryavada means the effect PRE-EXISTS in cause — 'completely new creation unrelated to causal substance' is the OPPOSITE of Satkaryavada; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect — select option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 deliberately describes Satkaryavada using language appropriate to Asatkaryavada. This reversed-causation trap catches students who know both terms exist but have not memorised their precise meanings, causing them to accept the inversion without checking the definition.
solution.final_explanation:
The debate between Satkaryavada and Asatkaryavada is the defining metaphysical disagreement between Samkhya and Vaisheshika.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Vaisheshika's Asatkaryavada (also called Arambhavada) holds that the effect (e.g., a pot) does not pre-exist in its cause (clay). It is a genuinely new entity brought into existence by atomic combination. This is why Vaisheshika's causal theory supports its pluralistic ontology.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Satkaryavada is Samkhya's theory and holds the exact opposite — the effect pre-exists in an unmanifest (Avyakta) form within the cause. Creation is the manifestation of what already existed. There is no ex nihilo creation in Samkhya — Prakriti always existed and simply becomes manifest.

Value Addition:
• Satkaryavada → 'Sat' = existing; the effect already IS (Sat) in the cause.
• Asatkaryavada → 'Asat' = not existing; the effect does NOT yet exist (Asat) in the cause.
• Advaita Vedanta's Vivartavada is a third position: the world is not even a real transformation but an apparent one.

solution.concept_anchor: Vyapti — logical backbone of Nyaya inference
solution.strong_distractor: a — Paksha is a well-known Nyaya term (the subject of inference — e.g., 'the hill') and students may confuse the 'subject of inference' with its 'logical basis.'
elimination_logic: The blank requires the term for the 'invariable concomitance' or universal relationship that must hold for inference to be valid.
Eliminate option a: Paksha is the subject of the inference (e.g., 'the hill') — not the logical relationship.
Eliminate option c: Sadhya is the property to be proved (e.g., 'fire') — the conclusion, not the logical principle.
Eliminate option d: Hetu is the reason/middle term (e.g., 'smoke') — not the invariable relationship.
Confirm option b: Vyapti is the invariable concomitance — 'wherever smoke is, fire is' — the universal law underpinning inference.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Hetu (the reason/mark) is the strongest distractor because students conflate 'what makes inference work' with 'the specific reason used.' Hetu is the particular evidence; Vyapti is the universal law that makes that evidence valid. Missing this distinction causes selection of option d.
solution.final_explanation:
Nyaya's theory of inference requires a universal law to be established before a valid inference can be drawn.

• Option (a) Paksha: The subject of inference (e.g., 'the hill' in the classic smoke-fire example) — not the universal relationship.
• Option (b) Vyapti: Correct. Vyapti is the invariable concomitance — the universal law (e.g., 'wherever there is smoke, there is fire') that underpins the entire inference. Without Vyapti, Anumana is impossible.
• Option (c) Sadhya: The property being proved — the conclusion (e.g., 'fire' on the hill) — not the logical principle.
• Option (d) Hetu: The specific reason or mark (e.g., 'smoke') that points to the conclusion — one element of the syllogism, not the universal law itself.

Value Addition:
• Vyapti must be established through repeated, uncontradicted observation — not a single instance.
• 'Sati vyaptau anumanam' — inference requires established Vyapti.
• Naiyayikas debated whether Vyapti can be known through perception or only through induction.

solution.concept_anchor: Vaisheshika — pluralistic realism, not idealism
solution.strong_distractor: b — Advaita Vedanta and Vaisheshika are both Astika schools, and students who know Vaisheshika is 'not materialist' may assume it is idealist like Advaita without checking the precise ontological category.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: Vaisheshika does NOT deny the external world — it is a realist school; this is the Buddhist Vijnanavada (idealist) position.
Eliminate option b: Vaisheshika is NOT idealistic — Advaita Vedanta is idealistic (or at least phenomenalist); Vaisheshika is a pluralistic realism.
Eliminate option c: Vaisheshika accepts multiple substances including non-material ones (Atman, Manas, Time, Space) — it is not materialist.
Confirm option d: Vaisheshika is correctly paired with pluralistic realism — multiple independently real substances (nine Dravyas) constitute the world.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option b attracts students who correctly eliminate Buddhist idealism and materialist positions but then default to Advaita idealism as the next possibility. The trap is that Vaisheshika's specific classification — pluralistic realism — requires positive knowledge, not just elimination of the most obvious wrong answers.
solution.final_explanation:
Correctly classifying Vaisheshika's metaphysical position requires precision.

• Option (a): Incorrectly pairs Vaisheshika with idealism denying external reality — this describes Buddhist Vijnanavada/Yogachara, which Vaisheshika actively refuted.
• Option (b): Incorrectly pairs Vaisheshika with the idealism of Advaita Vedanta — Advaita holds Brahman as the sole reality and the world as Maya. Vaisheshika holds multiple substances as genuinely real.
• Option (c): Incorrectly pairs Vaisheshika with materialism — Vaisheshika accepts non-material substances like Atman, Manas, Time, and Space, making it non-materialist.
• Option (d): Correct. Vaisheshika is a pluralistic realism — it holds that multiple independently real substances (nine Dravyas) constitute the universe; the external world exists independently of any perceiving mind.

Value Addition:
• Vaisheshika's realism extends to universals (Samanya) — even abstract class properties exist objectively.
• This places Vaisheshika in direct opposition to both Buddhist idealism and Buddhist nominalism.
• The pluralism (multiple substances) distinguishes it from Advaita's monism.

solution.concept_anchor: Upamana as unique Nyaya Pramana

statement_analysis.statement: Upamana (comparison/analogy) is a distinct Pramana in Nyaya that is not recognised as an independent source of valid knowledge in the Samkhya system.
statement_analysis.reason: Samkhya accepts only three Pramanas — Pratyaksha, Anumana, and Shabda — and does not include Upamana. Nyaya's inclusion of Upamana as a fourth, distinct Pramana is its unique epistemological contribution.

statement_analysis.statement: In Nyaya, Shabda (testimony) as a Pramana is restricted exclusively to Vedic utterances and does not include the testimony of reliable human beings.
statement_analysis.reason: Shabda in Nyaya includes both Vedic (Vaidika) testimony and the testimony of reliable (Apta) persons — it is not restricted to Vedic texts alone. The reliability of the speaker (Aptatva) is the key criterion.

statement_analysis.statement: The Nyaya school's five-membered syllogism includes an example (Udaharana) that explicitly states the universal rule through a concrete case, distinguishing it from purely abstract Western syllogistic forms.
statement_analysis.reason: The Udaharana step provides a concrete example (e.g., 'as in a kitchen, where there is smoke, there is fire'), which combines a universal statement with an illustrative case — unlike Aristotelian syllogism's purely abstract universal premise.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know Shabda includes Vedic authority may over-extend this to think Vedic testimony is the ONLY type, marking Statement 2 as correct and selecting option d.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Samkhya has three Pramanas — no Upamana — making Nyaya's inclusion of Upamana its unique contribution; Statement 1 is correct.
Examine Statement 2: Shabda in Nyaya includes both Vaidika (Vedic) and Laukika (secular reliable testimony) — not restricted to Vedas alone; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: The Udaharana as a concrete universal example is a genuine feature of Nyaya syllogism not found in Aristotelian form; Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits Nyaya's association with Vedic orthodoxy. Students assume that since Nyaya accepts Vedic authority, Shabda must mean only Vedic testimony. The scope-extension trap adds 'exclusively' — Nyaya actually accepts reliable human testimony (Laukika Shabda) as equally valid.
solution.final_explanation:
Nyaya's epistemological sophistication is shown in the fine distinctions within each Pramana.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Upamana is Nyaya's distinctive fourth Pramana — knowledge of a new object through its resemblance to a known one. Samkhya excludes it, accepting only three Pramanas.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Shabda in Nyaya is not limited to Vedic texts. It includes testimony of any Apta (reliable, trustworthy person). The reliability criterion applies to human testimony too — making Shabda a broad epistemological category.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Udaharana step in the Nyaya syllogism provides a concrete illustration (e.g., 'like a kitchen') alongside the universal rule, making it both deductive and inductive in character — unlike the purely formal Aristotelian structure.

Value Addition:
• Upamana is often explained through the gavaya (wild cow) example — a forest dweller learns what a gavaya looks like by being told 'it resembles a domestic cow.'
• Nyaya distinguishes Aptatva (reliability) in Shabda — the speaker must have direct knowledge and honest intent.
• The Udaharana in Nyaya syllogism foreshadows the role of examples in scientific reasoning.

solution.concept_anchor: Nine Dravyas of Vaisheshika — which is not a Dravya
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may doubt whether 'Space (Dik)' is among the nine Dravyas since it seems like an abstract concept rather than a 'substance', making them select it as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Recall the nine Dravyas: Earth, Water, Fire, Air, Akasha (Ether), Kala (Time), Dik (Space), Atman (Self), Manas (Mind).
Verify option b: Kala (Time) — confirmed ninth Dravya.
Verify option c: Dik (Space) — confirmed Dravya in Vaisheshika.
Verify option d: Manas (Mind) — confirmed Dravya.
Check option a: Samanya (Universal/Class essence) is a Padartha (category), not a Dravya (substance) — it is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Samanya is routinely taught alongside the nine Dravyas in Vaisheshika texts, making students familiar with both lists but unsure of their categories. Students who doubt Kala (Time) or Dik (Space) as 'substances' will select them as the odd one out instead of correctly identifying Samanya as a category (Padartha), not a substance (Dravya).
solution.final_explanation:
Vaisheshika distinguishes its nine Dravyas (substances) from the broader Padarthas (categories).

• Option (a) Samanya (Universal): This is the ODD ONE OUT. Samanya is not a Dravya but a Padartha — it is the universal class essence (e.g., 'cowness') that creates resemblance among individuals. Universals are real in Vaisheshika but they are not substances.
• Option (b) Kala (Time): One of the nine Dravyas — an eternal, all-pervading, non-atomic substance that accounts for temporal relations.
• Option (c) Dik (Space): One of the nine Dravyas — an eternal, all-pervading substance accounting for spatial relations and directional distinctions.
• Option (d) Manas (Mind): One of the nine Dravyas — an atomic-sized, eternal mediating substance for each individual.

Value Addition:
• The nine Dravyas cover both material (four elements) and non-material (Atman, Manas, Akasha, Kala, Dik) substances.
• Vaisheshika's inclusion of Time and Space as substances (not just relations) is philosophically distinctive.
• Dravya (substance) is the first and most fundamental of the six/seven Padarthas.

solution.concept_anchor: Nyaya refutation of Buddhist momentariness — enduring substance
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true and know Nyaya opposed Buddhism will assume R explains A without examining whether the specific causal mechanism is correct.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Nyaya-Vaisheshika argued against Buddhist Kshanabhangavada (doctrine of momentariness), contending that substances endure through time.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. Udayana's Nyayakusumanjali does provide logical proofs for God's existence and systematically refutes Buddhist atheism.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. Nyaya's refutation of momentariness (A) is based on its doctrine of enduring substance (Dravya) and its realist ontology — not on proofs for God's existence. Udayana's theistic arguments address a different Buddhist claim (atheism), not momentariness. These are two distinct philosophical disputes.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A — select option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both A and R describe genuine aspects of Nyaya-Vaisheshika's opposition to Buddhism, but they address different Buddhist doctrines. A addresses momentariness; R addresses atheism. Students who see 'anti-Buddhist stance' in both will assume R explains A, missing that these are independent philosophical disputes addressed by different arguments.
solution.final_explanation:
Nyaya-Vaisheshika's engagement with Buddhist philosophy was multi-dimensional, targeting different doctrines separately.

Assertion (A): Nyaya-Vaisheshika rejected Kshanabhangavada — the Buddhist doctrine that all existents are momentary flashes with no enduring substance. Nyaya argued that enduring substances (Dravyas) are necessary to explain continuity of identity, causal efficacy, and the coherence of experience. This is factually correct.

Reason (R): Udayana's Nyayakusumanjali (10th–11th CE) provides logical proofs for God's existence, addressing Buddhist atheism — this is also factually correct.

Causal relationship: R does not explain A. The refutation of momentariness is grounded in Nyaya's substance-attribute ontology — not in theistic proofs. These are independent philosophical arguments against different Buddhist claims. Option b is correct.

Value Addition:
• Kshanabhangavada: Buddhist doctrine that each moment of existence is distinct — no persistent self or substance.
• Nyaya countered this with the concept of Dravya as a persistent substratum that endures through change.
• Udayana targeted Buddhist atheism separately through the cosmological argument (God as organiser of atoms).
• This illustrates that Nyaya-Vaisheshika's anti-Buddhist polemics covered epistemology, ontology, and theology.

solution.concept_anchor: Navya-Nyaya — Gangesa, Mithila, Nabadwip

statement_analysis.statement: Gangesa Upadhyaya, who founded the Navya-Nyaya school in the 13th century CE, was associated with the Mithila region.
statement_analysis.reason: Gangesa Upadhyaya was from Mithila (present-day northern Bihar/Nepal region) — Mithila was the original centre of Navya-Nyaya scholarship.

statement_analysis.statement: The Navya-Nyaya school later spread to Nabadwip in Bengal, where it flourished as a centre of advanced logical studies.
statement_analysis.reason: Nabadwip (Navadvipa) in Bengal became the second major centre of Navya-Nyaya, where it continued to develop through the medieval period.

statement_analysis.statement: Navya-Nyaya's primary innovation was the rejection of the four Pramanas of classical Nyaya and the substitution of a new set of valid sources of knowledge.
statement_analysis.reason: Navya-Nyaya did not reject the four Pramanas — it retained the classical Nyaya framework but developed an extremely precise technical metalanguage (e.g., Avacchedaka, Pratiyogita) for analysing these sources more rigorously.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who are unfamiliar with Navya-Nyaya's content may assume it made radical changes to the Pramana list, accepting Statement 3 and marking all three correct.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Gangesa and Mithila as the original Navya-Nyaya centre is established fact — Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: Nabadwip as the second major centre of Navya-Nyaya is well documented — Statement 2 is correct.
Examine Statement 3: Navya-Nyaya refined the analysis of Pramanas using technical language — it did NOT replace or reject the four Pramanas; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect — select option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the fact that Navya-Nyaya introduced highly technical new vocabulary. Students assume new terminology means new Pramanas — but the school retained classical Nyaya's four Pramanas entirely. The innovation was analytical method, not epistemological content.
solution.final_explanation:
Navya-Nyaya represents the medieval reformation of classical Nyaya logic.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Gangesa Upadhyaya, the 13th century CE founder, was from Mithila — the original and primary centre of Navya-Nyaya scholarship.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Nabadwip (Bengal) emerged as a major secondary centre where Navya-Nyaya thrived through the 15th–17th centuries.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Navya-Nyaya retained the four Pramanas (Pratyaksha, Anumana, Upamana, Shabda). Its innovation was the development of an extraordinarily precise technical vocabulary — terms like Avacchedaka (limitor), Pratiyogita (counter-positiveness) — to analyse these Pramanas with greater rigour, not to replace them.

Value Addition:
• Navya-Nyaya's technical language influenced Sanskrit commentarial literature across disciplines including Vedanta, Mimamsa, and law.
• Tattvachintamani deals primarily with Pramanas — especially Anumana — in unprecedented detail.
• The school is sometimes compared to formal logic in Western philosophy for its precision.

solution.concept_anchor: Samavaya — inseparable inherence as Padartha
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Samavaya is a relational concept may confuse it with Samyoga (another relational concept), thinking both are subsumed under Guna (quality).
elimination_logic: Identify what Samavaya is: it is the inseparable, permanent relation between substance and quality, whole and parts, universal and particular.
Eliminate option a: Samavaya is not a type of Dravya — Dravyas are substances; Samavaya is a distinct ontological category.
Eliminate option b: Samavaya is not a type of Guna — Gunas are qualities; Samyoga (contact) is a Guna, not Samavaya.
Eliminate option c: Samavaya is not a subtype of Karma — Karmas are actions/motions.
Confirm option d: Samavaya is one of the original six Padarthas of Kanada — the inseparable inherence relation.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students confuse Samavaya with Samyoga. Samyoga (contact) is a Guna; Samavaya is a separate Padartha. This distinction is the core of the trap — both are relational, but one is a quality and the other is a fundamental ontological category.
solution.final_explanation:
Samavaya is one of the most philosophically significant concepts in Vaisheshika.

• Option (a): Samavaya is not a Dravya. Dravyas are the nine substances (Earth, Water, Fire, Air, Akasha, Kala, Dik, Atman, Manas).
• Option (b): Samavaya is not a Guna (quality). Samyoga (contact) is a Guna — but Samavaya is entirely different. Samavaya is the inseparable, inherent connection between a substance and its quality, between a whole and its parts, or between a universal and its particular instances.
• Option (c): Karma (action) includes five types of physical motion. Samavaya has nothing to do with motion.
• Option (d): Correct. Samavaya is the sixth of Kanada's original six Padarthas — the category of inseparable inherence (Ayutasiddha sambandha). It is what holds quality in substance, universal in particular, and part in whole — permanently and inseparably.

Value Addition:
• The classic Samavaya example: colour (Guna) inheres in a cloth (Dravya) — they cannot be physically separated without destroying the relationship.
• Samavaya itself is one — there is only one relation of inherence, not multiple instances.
• Samyoga vs Samavaya: a book on a table is Samyoga (separable); colour in cloth is Samavaya (inseparable).

solution.concept_anchor: Nyaya liberation path — Tattvajnana to Apavarga

statement_analysis.statement: In Nyaya philosophy, liberation (Apavarga) is achieved when the individual Atman merges with the universal Brahman, resulting in the cessation of individual identity.
statement_analysis.reason: Nyaya does not teach merger of Atman with Brahman — this is Advaita Vedanta's conception. Nyaya's Apavarga involves the cessation of all pain while the individual Atman retains its distinct individuality (pluralism is maintained).

statement_analysis.statement: The path to liberation in Nyaya involves the attainment of Tattvajnana (right knowledge of the 16 categories), which destroys false knowledge and thereby stops the cycle of rebirth.
statement_analysis.reason: Nyaya holds that liberation begins with right knowledge — knowing the true nature of the self, world, and God dispels ignorance, removes attachment and aversion, and halts rebirth.

statement_analysis.statement: The liberated state (Apavarga) in Nyaya is characterised by the complete absence of both suffering and any positive experiential state — the Atman exists in a state analogous to dreamless unconsciousness.
statement_analysis.reason: Nyaya's Moksha is explicitly negative — it is the termination of all duhkha (suffering) without any residual positive bliss or consciousness; the Atman in this state is without attributes, like a stone — sometimes described as 'stone-like' (pashana-kalpa).

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who are familiar with the Vedantic concept of liberation may assume Statement 1 describes a general feature of all Astika schools, not realising Nyaya explicitly rejects Atman-Brahman merger.
elimination_logic: Examine Statement 1: 'Atman merges with Brahman' is Advaita Vedanta's Moksha — Nyaya maintains individual Atman plurality even in liberation; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Examine Statement 2: Tattvajnana as the starting point of liberation in Nyaya is accurate — Statement 2 is correct.
Examine Statement 3: The 'stone-like' unconscious liberated Atman is a known Nyaya description — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statement 1 is incorrect — select option c (1 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 uses the phrase 'Atman merges with Brahman' — which sounds like a general Astika position but actually describes only Advaita Vedanta. Nyaya's pluralism means individual Atmans never merge. Students who equate Astika with Vedantic liberation will incorrectly accept Statement 1.
solution.final_explanation:
Nyaya's concept of liberation diverges sharply from Vedantic formulations.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Nyaya does not teach Atman-Brahman merger. This is the Advaitic concept. Nyaya is pluralistic — multiple individual Atmans exist eternally and remain distinct even in liberation. Apavarga is the cessation of pain for each individual Atman, not its dissolution into Brahman.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Nyaya liberation path: Tattvajnana (right knowledge of the 16 topics including Atman, God, Pramanas) → dispels Mithyajnana (false knowledge) → removes Raga/Dvesha (attachment/aversion) → stops Pravritti (activity) → ends rebirth → Apavarga.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The liberated Nyaya Atman is often described as 'stone-like' (pashana-kalpa) — freed from all pain but also from consciousness. This negative liberation has been criticised by Vedantins who see it as no better than death.

Value Addition:
• Vedantins criticised Nyaya's Apavarga: 'If liberation is unconsciousness, why prefer it to sleep?'
• The 16 Prameyas (objects of right knowledge) in Nyaya include Atman, body, senses, objects, cognition, mind, activity, fault, transmigration, fruit, suffering, and liberation.
• Knowing all 16 correctly is the entire soteriological programme of Nyaya.

solution.concept_anchor: Vaisheshika Padarthas — precise definitions of five categories
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Samanya means 'general/universal' and Vishesha means 'particular/special' may correctly place these two but swap Karma and Guna, since both are familiar from non-Vaisheshika contexts.
elimination_logic: Identify Dravya (A): Substance — the substratum in which qualities and actions inhere; e.g., earth, water, Atman — maps to item 3.
Identify Samanya (B): The universal or class essence — what makes all cows 'cow'; maps to item 1.
Identify Karma (C): Physical action or motion — not moral action in the everyday sense; maps to item 4.
Identify Vishesha (D): The ultimate differentiators of eternal substances (atoms, Atman) — what makes each atom distinct from every other; maps to item 2. This gives A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 — option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Karma-Guna swap is the primary distractor here. Students familiar with 'Guna' as qualities (from Samkhya's three Gunas) and 'Karma' as moral action may misassign these Vaisheshika Padarthas. In Vaisheshika, Karma is strictly physical motion — this technical usage must be distinguished from its colloquial and other philosophical meanings.
solution.final_explanation:
The six original Padarthas of Vaisheshika require precise definitional knowledge:

• A (Dravya) — 3 (Substratum in which qualities and actions inhere): Dravya is the foundational category — the nine substances that serve as the basis for all qualities and motions.
• B (Samanya) — 1 (Universal class essence creating resemblance among individuals): 'Cowness' is the Samanya inhering in all cows — it is the basis of classification and inference.
• C (Karma) — 4 (Physical motion or action of a substance): In Vaisheshika, Karma means physical movement — upward (Utkshepana), downward (Avakshepana), contraction, expansion, locomotion. Not moral action.
• D (Vishesha) — 2 (Ultimate differentiators making each eternal atom distinct from every other): Vishesha are the ultimate particulars — since atoms of the same element are otherwise identical, Vishesha account for their individuation.

Value Addition:
• The name of the school derives from Vishesha — the 'differentiator' is its unique philosophical contribution.
• Karma in Vaisheshika (motion) vs Karma in Vedanta (moral consequence) — a critical distinction across schools.
• Samanya exists at multiple levels — specific (e.g., cowness) and most general (existence/Being).

statement_analysis.statement: Charvaka (Lokayata) school — accepts Pratyaksha (perception) as its only Pramana.
statement_analysis.reason: Charvaka is a strict materialist school that rejects inference (Anumana) and testimony (Shabda) as unreliable, accepting only direct sensory perception.

statement_analysis.statement: Samkhya school — accepts Pratyaksha, Anumana, and Upamana as its three Pramanas.
statement_analysis.reason: Samkhya accepts three Pramanas — Pratyaksha, Anumana, and Shabda — not Upamana. Upamana is rejected by Samkhya and is instead distinctive to Nyaya.

statement_analysis.statement: Nyaya school — accepts Pratyaksha, Anumana, Upamana, and Shabda as its four Pramanas.
statement_analysis.reason: The four Pramanas of Nyaya are established fact — Upamana (comparison/analogy) is Nyaya's unique contribution among the Astika schools.

statement_analysis.statement: Mimamsa school — accepts six Pramanas, including Arthapatti (postulation) and Anupalabdhi (non-apprehension).
statement_analysis.reason: Mimamsa (specifically Purva Mimamsa) accepts six Pramanas: Pratyaksha, Anumana, Upamana, Shabda, Arthapatti, and Anupalabdhi.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Samkhya has three Pramanas but misremember the third as Upamana (rather than Shabda) will count three pairs as correct and select option c.
elimination_logic: Pair 1 — Charvaka and one Pramana: Charvaka accepts only Pratyaksha — correct.
Pair 2 — Samkhya and three Pramanas including Upamana: Samkhya's three are Pratyaksha, Anumana, Shabda — NOT Upamana; this pair is incorrect.
Pair 3 — Nyaya and four Pramanas: Pratyaksha, Anumana, Upamana, Shabda — correct.
Pair 4 — Mimamsa and six Pramanas: Including Arthapatti and Anupalabdhi — correct.
Three of four pairs are correct — select option c (Only three).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Pair 2 exploits the most common error in Pramana comparison: students know Samkhya has three Pramanas but substitute Upamana for Shabda. Since Upamana is taught as Nyaya's distinctive contribution, and Samkhya is taught alongside Nyaya, the confusion transfers easily.
solution.final_explanation:
The number and types of Pramanas vary significantly across Indian philosophical schools:

| School | Pramanas Accepted |
|---|---|
| Charvaka | Pratyaksha only |
| Samkhya | Pratyaksha, Anumana, Upamana [INCORRECT — should be Shabda] |
| Nyaya | Pratyaksha, Anumana, Upamana, Shabda |
| Mimamsa | Six including Arthapatti, Anupalabdhi |

• Pair 1 — Correct: Charvaka accepts only Pratyaksha.
• Pair 2 — Incorrect: Samkhya's third Pramana is Shabda, not Upamana. Upamana is Nyaya's distinctive contribution that Samkhya excludes.
• Pair 3 — Correct: Nyaya's four Pramanas are correctly listed.
• Pair 4 — Correct: Mimamsa adds Arthapatti and Anupalabdhi to reach six.

Three of four pairs correctly stated — option c.

Value Addition:
• Advaita Vedanta also accepts six Pramanas like Mimamsa.
• Vishishtadvaita accepts three; Dvaita accepts three.
• Buddhism (various schools) accepts 1–4 depending on the sub-school.

solution.concept_anchor: Abhava — seventh Padartha, not in Kanada original
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Abhava is part of Vaisheshika philosophy but are unaware of when it was added will assume it was in Kanada's original six, selecting option b.
elimination_logic: Identify the question: which statement about Abhava as Vaisheshika's seventh category is correct?
Eliminate option b: Abhava was NOT part of Kanada's original six — it was added by later commentators.
Eliminate option c: Abhava has four sub-types (Pragabhava, Pradhvamsabhava, Anyonyabhava, Atyantabhava) — not three.
Eliminate option d: Atyantabhava is absolute non-existence — not mutual non-existence; Anyonyabhava is mutual non-existence.
Confirm option a: Abhava was added as a seventh category by later commentators and was not part of Kanada's original enumeration.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option b exploits the common student error of conflating 'part of the Vaisheshika system' with 'part of Kanada's original text.' Abhava is genuine Vaisheshika philosophy but was introduced by later commentators — the distinction between Kanada's original six and the later seventh addition is the precise tested fact.
solution.final_explanation:
Abhava (non-existence) is a philosophically bold category — it treats non-being as a real ontological entity.

• Option (a): Correct. Abhava was added as the seventh Padartha by later Vaisheshika commentators — it is not found in Kanada's original Vaisheshika Sutras, which enumerate only six categories.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The temporal claim is wrong — Kanada's original six did not include Abhava. This is the key trap.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Abhava has four sub-types, not three: Pragabhava, Pradhvamsabhava, Anyonyabhava, and Atyantabhava.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Atyantabhava is absolute/eternal non-existence (e.g., sky-flower — never exists). Anyonyabhava is mutual non-existence (e.g., a cow is not a horse). The descriptions are swapped.

Value Addition:
• The four types cover temporal non-existence (Pragabhava, Pradhvamsabhava), relational non-existence (Anyonyabhava), and absolute non-existence (Atyantabhava).
• Making non-existence a positive ontological category is Vaisheshika's way of giving logical tools for negation.
• Pragabhava has no beginning (the pot didn't exist before creation began) but has an end; Pradhvamsabhava has a beginning but no end.
